title: Ὄνος καὶ κύων συνοδοιποροῦντες
titleEn: The Donkey and the Dog Travelling Together
part: The Donkey and the Dog Travelling Together (Chambry 276 · Perry 264)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 276 (= Perry 264). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος καὶ κύων ἐν ταὐτῷ ὡδοιπόρουν.
sentences.tr: Onos kai kyōn en tautōi hōdoiporoun.
sentences.l: A donkey and a dog were travelling in the same place.
sentences.i: A donkey and a dog were making a journey together.
sentences.n: ἐν ταὐτῷ again, the crasis of τῷ αὐτῷ, 'in the same place' and so 'in company' — the same opening as fable 272. ὡδοιπόρουν is the imperfect of ὁδοιπορέω: the augment contracts with the initial ο- to give ω-, and the rough breathing rides on it unchanged.

sentences.t: Εὑρόντες δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς ἐσφραγισμένον γραμμάτιον, ὁ ὄνος λαβὼν καὶ ἀναρρήξας τὴν σφραγῖδα καὶ ἀναπτύξας, διεξῄει εἰς ἐπήκοον τοῦ κυνός.
sentences.tr: Heurontes de epi gēs esphragismenon grammation, ho onos labōn kai anarrēxas tēn sphragida kai anaptyxas, diexēiei eis epēkoon tou kynos.
sentences.l: And having found a sealed document on the ground, the donkey, having taken it and having broken the seal and having unrolled it, was going through it within the dog's hearing.
sentences.i: They found a sealed document lying on the ground, and the donkey took it, broke the seal, unrolled it and read it out where the dog could hear.
sentences.n: The aorist-participle chain is the fable's usual engine: four participles stack up the whole action and only the last verb, διεξῄει, is finite. ἀναπτύσσω is to unfold or unroll, the proper word for opening a book-roll, and διέξειμι of a written thing is to go right through it aloud. εἰς ἐπήκοον with the genitive is 'within earshot of'.

sentences.t: Περὶ βοσκημάτων δὲ ἐτύγχανε τὰ γράμματα χόρτου τε, φημί, καὶ κριθῆς καὶ ἀχύρου.
sentences.tr: Peri boskēmatōn de etynchane ta grammata chortou te, phēmi, kai krithēs kai achyrou.
sentences.l: And the writing happened to be about fodder — of hay, I mean, and barley and chaff.
sentences.n: τυγχάνω normally wants a supplementary participle; here ὄντα is simply left out and the περί-phrase does the work alone. φημί is dropped in parenthetically, 'I mean' — the narrator breaking in on his own sentence, which is rare in these fables. βόσκημα is properly the thing that is fed — usually the grazing beast; here the three genitives that follow, hay and barley and chaff, force the other sense, the feed itself.

sentences.t: Ἀηδῶς οὖν ὁ κύων, τοῦ ὄνου ταῦτα διεξιόντος, διέκειτο· ἔνθεν δὴ καὶ ἔφησε τῷ ὄνῳ· « Ὑπόβαθι, φίλτατε, μικρόν, μή τι καὶ περὶ κρεῶν καὶ ὀστέων εὕρῃς διαλαμβάνων. »
sentences.tr: Aēdōs oun ho kyōn, tou onou tauta diexiontos, diekeito· enthen dē kai ephēse tōi onōi· « Hypobathi, philtate, mikron, mē ti kai peri kreōn kai osteōn heurēis dialambanōn. »
sentences.l: Ill-pleased, then, was the dog while the donkey was going through these things; and thereupon he said to the donkey: « Step down a little, dearest fellow, on the chance you may find something about meat and bones too, taking it up piece by piece. »
sentences.i: The dog, then, took it badly while the donkey was reading these things out; and so he said to the donkey: « Go a little further down, my dear fellow — as you work through it bit by bit you may find something about meat and bones as well. »
sentences.n: ἀηδῶς διάκειμαι is the ordinary Greek for being displeased: διάκειμαι says only 'be in a state' and the adverb carries the whole feeling. Ὑπόβαθι is the aorist imperative of ὑποβαίνω, 'step down', used here of moving further down the roll. μή with the subjunctive is not fear but the cautious 'perhaps you may' — the dog is hoping for what he names, not dreading it. διαλαμβάνων is nominative and belongs to the donkey, the subject of εὕρῃς: διαλαμβάνω is to take a thing in separate portions, so he is working through the roll piece by piece — a different verb from the διεξιόντος just before, which is reading it straight through.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὄνος ἅπαν τὸ γραμμάτιον διεξελθὼν καὶ μηδὲν εὑρηκὼς ὧν ὁ κύων ἐζήτει, ἀντέφησεν αὖθις ὁ κύων· « Βάλε κατὰ γῆς, ὡς ἀδόκιμον πάντη, φίλε, τυγχάνον. »
sentences.tr: Ho de onos hapan to grammation diexelthōn kai mēden heurēkōs hōn ho kyōn ezētei, antephēsen authis ho kyōn· « Bale kata gēs, hōs adokimon pantē, phile, tynchanon. »
sentences.l: And the donkey having gone right through the whole document and having found none of the things the dog was looking for, the dog said back to him again: « Throw it down on the ground, since it is, my friend, altogether worthless. »
sentences.i: And when the donkey had gone right through the whole document and found none of what the dog was after, the dog spoke up again: « Throw it down on the ground, my friend; the thing is worthless through and through. »
sentences.n: The sentence is broken as it stands: ὁ δὲ ὄνος and the two nominative participles set up a subject that never receives its verb, since ἀντέφησεν has ὁ κύων. Ordinary Greek would have used a genitive absolute, τοῦ δὲ ὄνου … διεξελθόντος. Chambry prints it as it has come down and it is left standing here. ὡς with the participle τυγχάνον gives the reason as the dog's own view of the matter; πάντη is 'in every way'. Chambry prints no moral for this fable, so the page ends with the dog's verdict.
